Q: How to determine incoming TLS version for Azure Storage A:

A quick way to perform this audit is create an Azure Policy that checks for Diagnostic Settings on each Storage Service, apply to the desired scope, and create a remediation task that will go ahead and create the missing Diagnostic Settings. Then query the logs.

Note that StorageFileLogs don't actually emit TlsVersion despite the property existing and being documented. Seems like a bad oversight. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/reference/tables/storagefilelogs https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5721993/tls-version-in-azure-log-is-blank?utm_source=chatgpt.com

union withsource=TableName
    StorageBlobLogs, 
    StorageTableLogs, 
    StorageFileLogs, 
    StorageQueueLogs,
    (AzureDiagnostics 
     | where ResourceProvider == "MICROSOFT.STORAGE" 
     | where Category == "Transaction"
     // Safely check for TlsVersion in various possible column names
     | extend TlsVersion = coalesce(
         tostring(column_ifexists("TlsVersion_s", "")), 
         tostring(column_ifexists("tlsVersion_s", "")),
         "Unknown"
       )
     | extend AccountName = Resource)
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) and TlsVersion != "TLS 1.2" and TlsVersion != "TLS 1.3"
| summarize count() by TlsVersion, AccountName, TableName
| order by TlsVersion, AccountName, TableName

Q: Conflicting typedef 'long int t4_i32’ vs. 'long t4_i32' vs. 'int t4_i32' A:

Built-in C++ arithmetic (floating point, and integral) types don't have universally defined sizes or bit width. C++ only defines a strict weak order on their relative sizes. For integral types, the ascending order is:

signed char, signed short int, signed int, signed long int, signed long long int.

The signed and int keywords are optional, iff the type name string has at least one keyword, ecxept for char which is distinct from both signed char and unsigned char. Same order applies to unsigned counterparts. Each of the integral types is promised to be not smaller in size than the previous one with same signedness. So, depending on platform int might have the same size as short, or long. But the same size doesn't imply same size. All these 2×5 integral types are distinct from each other, and from integral character representation types(char, wchar_t, char8_t, char16_t, char32_). Compilers may add extra none-standard types to the list.

Aside from seemingly incorrect assumptions about built in integeral types and their sizes, you are also trying to reinvent the wheel. All you need is to include <cstdint>. It will define fixed sized integeral types as proper aliases and save you the effort. Other than std::[u]intN_t family, you have std::[u]int_fastN_t, as well as std::[u]int_leastN_t family and a few more alaises. Many of these aliase types overlap and refer to same type. But, ordinary, fast, and least types are generally distinct; optimized for actual size vs computation speed and/or alignment.

Besides all the above, an arithmetic library had better be written in generic form using C++20 <concepts>, and <limits> header files. Since integral types share many similarities, defining templates instead of individual overloads DRYs the code base:

template<std::integral int_t>
auto scale_then_offset(int_t a, int_t b, int_c)
{ return a * b + c; };

In case of providing an overload for specific integral types, you need avoid aliases and use built-in type names. Because overlapping fixed width integeral alaises may cause multiple-definition errors.

All in all, defining such generic, and abstract libraries requires certain level of C++ proficiency. Or the codebase will be flooded with UB, on top of annoyingly many compile errors. Be smart, avoid trouble. In C++ "Less is more" very often.

Q: Razor Pages is not showing the ErrorMessage on asp-validation-for tag helper A:

A few hours later I've figure out the problem. I forgot to add the BindPropertyAttribute to my properties:

[BindProperty]
[Required(ErrorMessage = "User Name is a required field.")]
public String UserName { get; set; } = String.Empty;

Q: Why is my VS Code always opened with the default profile? A:

Late to the party, but I just came across this issue myself. I just wanted to post some clarifying instructions for the process listed by @omsharp. I think that the other more simple answers listed will accomplish the same thing, but I wanted to list the details on this process in case anyone is having issues with getting one of the other more simple solutions to work.

I did come across a few bumps in the process but was able to get through it to work.

NOTE: I'm using v1.80.1 per limitations imposed by being in a work environment. Newer/older versions might behave differently, but this is good to have for reference at least.

Here's the process I went through step by step:

  1. click on the gear icon at the bottom of the primary side bar

  2. click on "Profiles"

  3. Ensure you are on the profile you want to set as the default profile, you'll know because there will be a check mark next to the profile name.

  4. click on "Export Profile..."

  5. this will bring up "PROFILES:<your profile name>" in the primary side bar with two dropdowns: "Settings" and "UI State" with checkboxes to the left of them. Make sure both of these checkboxes are checked.

  6. click the "Export" button right below these dropdowns

  7. this will open an "Export Profile" box asking for you to name it. Name it as "Default"

  8. this will open an "Export 'Default' profile as..." with the options of "GitHub" and "Local". click on "Local" and save the profile wherever you want on your local machine

  9. repeat steps 1 and 2 to get back into the "Profiles" menu

  10. click on "Import Profile..."

  11. this brings up a "Create Profile from Profile Template..." box. Click on "Create from profile template file"

  12. in the window that pops up, navigate to where you saved the profile you exported as "Default" and select it, then click the "Open" button on the window

  13. this will open "PROFILES:DEFAULT" just like from step 5 but this time it will say "PROFILES:DEFAULT" instead of "PROFILES:<your profile name>"

  14. click "Create Profile"

  15. this will then show popup saying "Profile with name 'Default' already exists. Do you want to overwrite it?" with 3 buttons: "Create New Profile", "Cancel" and "Overwrite". click on "Overwrite"

    Now your Default profile will be overwritten with the profile you exported as "Default". Every time you open VS Code it will use your desired default profile settings. Hope this helps.
